'''Robert Geoffrey William Anderson''', {{Post-nominals|country=GBR|size=100%|sep=,|FSA|FRSE|FRSC}} (born 2 May 1944) is a British [[museum curator]] and historian of chemistry. He has interests in the history of chemistry, including the history of [[Instrumentation|scientific instrumentation]], the work of [[Joseph Black]] and [[Joseph Priestley]], the history of [[museums]], and the involvement of the [[working class]] in [[material culture]].<ref name="Cambridge"/><ref name="Bowman"/> He has been Keeper at the [[Science Museum, London]], and Director of the [[National Museums of Scotland]], and the [[British Museum]], [[London]],<ref name=Wotiz>John W. Wotiz, [http://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ed072p708 "A Conversation with Robert G. Anderson: Eminent Chemist and Director of the British Museum"], ''[[Journal of Chemical Education]]'', 72(8), p. 708, August 1995. [[ACS Publications]]. {{doi|10.1021/ed072p708}}.</ref> and president and CEO of the Chemical Heritage Foundation (now the [[Science History Institute]]) in [[Philadelphia]].<ref name="Everts"/>

==Education==
Anderson was born 2 May 1944 to Herbert Patrick Anderson and Kathleen Diana Burns.<ref>"ANDERSON, Robert Geoffrey William", ''[[Who's Who 2013]]'', A & C Black, an imprint of Bloomsbury Publishing plc, 2013; online edn, Oxford University Press, Dec 2012; online edn, Nov 2012 [http://www.ukwhoswho.com/view/article/oupww/whoswho/U5487 accessed 26 Sept 2013]</ref><ref name="Europa">{{cite book|last1=Publications|first1=Europa|title=The international who's who 2014|date=2013|publisher=Europa Publications|location=London|isbn=978-1857436846|page=47|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sR4Ch1dMe8IC&pg=PA47|chapter=Anderson, Robert Geoffrey William |accessdate=23 May 2016}}</ref> Anderson was educated at [[Woodhouse Grammar School]],{{cn|date=February 2026}} a former state grammar school in [[Finchley]] in North London, followed by [[St John's College, Oxford]]. He completed his B.A. in chemistry in 1966, and his B.Sc., and his Doctor of Philosophy (D. Phil.) in 1970. He studied the electrical conduction in free radical solutions and inelastic scattering of neutrons from adsorbed molecules.<ref name="Illinois">{{cite web|title=Robert G. W. Anderson (1944–)|url=http://www.scs.illinois.edu/~mainzv/HIST/awards/Dexter%20Papers/AndesonDexterBioJJB.pdf|website=University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign School of Chemical Sciences|accessdate=23 May 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180513234722/http://www.scs.illinois.edu/~mainzv/HIST/awards/Dexter%20Papers/AndesonDexterBioJJB.pdf|archive-date=13 May 2018}}</ref><ref name="OSU">{{cite web|last1=Anderson|first1=Robert|title=Circa 1951: Presenting Science to the British Public|url=http://scarc.library.oregonstate.edu/events/2007paulingconference/video-s2-3-anderson.html|website=Oregon State University|accessdate=23 May 2016}}</ref>

==Life and career==
Anderson joined the [[Royal Scottish Museum]] as an Assistant Keeper in 1970. In 1975, he moved to the chemistry department of the [[Science Museum, London]]. He became an Assistant Keeper of Chemistry. One of his challenges in 1976 was to incorporate materials from the history of medicine collection of the [[Wellcome Museum|Wellcome Collection]] of the History of Medicine, which were acquired as a permanent loan.<ref name="Gardner">{{cite journal|last1=Gardner|first1=A|last2=Kleinitz|first2=Cornelia|title=Interview with Dr. Robert Anderson, Director of the British Museum. Conducted 15/6/00|journal=Papers from the Institute of Archaeology|volume=11|pages=7|doi=10.5334/pia.150|year=2000|doi-access=free}}</ref> He organised a conference and edited "an excellent and detailed account"<ref name="Selwyn">{{cite journal|last1=Selwyn|first1=Sydney|title=The Early Years of the Edinburgh Medical School|journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of Medicine|date=1977|volume=70|issue=6|page=452|pmc=1543201|doi=10.1177/003591577707000649}}</ref> to celebrate the 250th Anniversary of the Faculty of Medicine of the University of Edinburgh, ''The Early Years of the Edinburgh Medical School.''<ref name="Early">{{cite book|editor-last1=Anderson|editor-first1=R.G.W.|editor-last2=Simpson|editor-first2=A.D.C.|title=The Early years of the Edinburgh Medical School : a symposium jointly organised by the Royal Scottish Museum and the Scottish Society of the History of Medicine in connection with the special exhibition Edinburgh and Medicine and the 250th anniversary of the foundation of the Faculty of Medicine of the University of Edinburgh, held in the Royal Scottish Museum, Chambers Street, Edinburgh, on 26th June 1976|date=1976|publisher=Royal Scottish Museum|location=Edinburgh|isbn=978-0900733109}}</ref> This was followed by a catalogue in 1978: ''The Playfair Collection and the Teaching of Chemistry at the University of Edinburgh 1713–1858.''<ref name="Playfair">{{cite book|last1=Anderson|first1=R.G.W.|title=The Playfair collection and the teaching of chemistry at the University of Edinburgh 1713-1858|date=1978|publisher=The Royal Scottish Museum|location=Edinburgh|isbn=9780900733161}}</ref> Anderson was also in charge of the renovation and expansion of the chemistry and industrial chemistry galleries in 1977.<ref name="Morris"/> He became keeper of chemistry, succeeded [[Frank Greenaway]] as director from 1980 to 1984.<ref name="Morris">{{cite journal|last1=Morris|first1=Peter|title=The Image of Chemistry Presented by the Science Museum, London in the Twentieth Century: An International Perspective|journal=Hyle: International Journal for Philosophy of Chemistry|date=2006|volume=12|issue=2|pages=215–239|url=http://www.hyle.org/journal/issues/12-2/morris.htm|accessdate=23 May 2016}}</ref> From 1981 he was a Member of [[Annals of Science]]'s Editorial Board.<ref>{{Cite book |first= |title=Who's Who 1995 |date=12 January 1995 |publisher=A & C Black Publishers Ltd |isbn=9780713639957 |edition=147th}}</ref>

Anderson returned to the [[Royal Scottish Museum]] as director from 1984 to 1985. When the Royal Scottish Museum amalgamated with National Museum of Antiquities in 1985, he became the director of the new [[National Museums of Scotland]] in [[Edinburgh]], a position he retained until 1992.<ref name="NMS">{{cite web|title=History of National Museums Scotland|url=http://www.nms.ac.uk/about-us/history-of-national-museums-scotland/|website=National Museums Scotland|accessdate=23 May 2016|archive-date=19 April 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170419081112/http://www.nms.ac.uk/about-us/history-of-national-museums-scotland|url-status=dead}}</ref>

[[File:P1050608 (5022061794).jpg |thumb|right| Queen Elizabeth II Great Court, [[British Museum]]]]
In 1992 Anderson joined the [[British Museum]] in London, where he was director from 1992 to 2002.<ref name="Bushby">{{cite news|last1=Bushby|first1=Helen|title=British Museum 'needs £10m boost'|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/entertainment/2069781.stm|access-date=23 May 2016|work=BBC|date=27 June 2002}}</ref> Anderson oversaw the £100 million millennium project redevelopment of the British Museum's [[Queen Elizabeth II Great Court]], designed by [[Norman Foster, Baron Foster of Thames Bank|Norman Foster]] and opened by the [[Elizabeth II of the United Kingdom|Queen]] on 6 December 2000.<ref name="BritishMuseumReview">{{cite web|date=2001|title=The British Museum Review|url=https://www.britishmuseum.org/pdf/annualreview0001.pdf|website=The British Museum|accessdate=23 May 2016}}</ref><ref name=Court>{{cite book|last1=Anderson|first1=Robert|title=The great court at the British Museum|date=2000|publisher=British Museum Press|location=London|isbn=978-0714127415|edition=Repr.}}</ref> Anderson was succeeded as director of the British Museum in 2002 by [[Neil MacGregor]].<ref name="BritishMuseum">{{cite web|title=Principal Librarians and Directors of the British Museum|url=https://www.britishmuseum.org/about_us/management/directors.aspx|website=British Museum|accessdate=23 May 2016}}</ref>

{{library resources box |by=yes| viaf=94486034}}
Anderson has been president of the Scientific Instrument Commission of the [[International Union of History and Philosophy of Science]] (1982–1997), and of the [[British Society for the History of Science]] (1988–1990).<ref name="Illinois"/> In 2004, Anderson became president of the [[Association of Independent Libraries]].<ref name="Bowman">{{cite book|last1=Bowman|first1=J. H.|title=British librarianship and information work : 1991-2000|date=2006|publisher=Ashgate|location=Hampshire|isbn=978-0-7546-4779-9|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=b_8GDAAAQBAJ&pg=PT145|accessdate=23 May 2016}}</ref>

Anderson has held visiting academic posts at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]], [[Princeton University]] and at the [[Centre for Research in the Arts, Social Sciences, and Humanities]] (CRASSH) at the [[Cambridge University|University of Cambridge]] (2002–2003).<ref>[http://www.crassh.cam.ac.uk/fellowships/2002-3/bioanderson.html CRASSH fellowship] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050904132003/http://www.crassh.cam.ac.uk/fellowships/2002-3/bioanderson.html |date=4 September 2005 }}, [[University of Cambridge]], 2002–2003.</ref> He is an Emeritus Fellow of [[Clare Hall, Cambridge]].<ref name="Cambridge">{{cite web|title=Dr Robert G W Anderson|url=http://www.clarehall.cam.ac.uk/our-people/dr-robert-g-w-anderson|website=Clare Hall, Cambridge|accessdate=23 May 2016|archive-date=8 June 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160608064348/https://www.clarehall.cam.ac.uk/our-people/dr-robert-g-w-anderson|url-status=dead}}</ref>

As of 28 July 2016, Anderson became interim president and CEO of the [[Chemical Heritage Foundation]] (now the [[Science History Institute]]),<ref name="Salisbury">{{cite news|last1=Salisbury|first1=Stephan|title=Chemical Heritage Foundation is morphing into the Science History Institute|url=http://www.philly.com/philly/entertainment/arts/chemical-heritage-foundation-science-history-institute-philadelphia-20180103.html|accessdate=1 February 2018|work=Philadelphia Inquirer|date=3 January 2018}}</ref> a history of science organization in [[Philadelphia]], Pennsylvania, USA. He succeeded German historian of science [[Carsten Reinhardt]]. On 11 January 2017, Anderson was named the institution's ongoing president and CEO.<ref name="Everts">{{cite news|last1=Everts|first1=Sarah|title=Chemical Heritage Foundation names Robert G. W. Anderson as president and CEO The former director of London's British Museum will take permanent helm of the chemical history organization|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/95/web/2017/01/Chemical-Heritage-Foundation-names-Robert-G-W-Anderson-as-president-and-CEO.html|accessdate=17 January 2017|work=Chemical & Engineering News|date=12 January 2017}}</ref> He was succeeded by [[David Allen Cole]] as of 20 May 2020.<ref name="Cole">{{cite web |title=David Cole President and CEO at Science History Institute |url=https://www.bizjournals.com/philadelphia/potmsearch/detail/submission/6484010/David_Cole |website=People on the Move |accessdate=26 May 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=David Allen Cole Named President and CEO of the Science History Institute |url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/news/david-cole-named-president-and-ceo |website=Science History Institute |date=18 May 2020 |accessdate=26 May 2020}}</ref>

Anderson has published at least 14 monographs or catalogues and at least 50 papers.<ref name="Illinois"/> His publications include works on the history of [[Instrumentation|scientific instrumentation]],<ref>{{cite book|editor-last1=Anderson|editor-first1=R. G. W.|editor-last2=Bennett|editor-first2=J. A.|editor-last3=Ryan|editor-first3=W. F.|title=Making instruments count : essays on historical scientific instruments presented to Gerard L'Estrange Turner|date=1993|publisher=Variorum|location=Aldershot, Hampshire|isbn=978-0860783947}}</ref> the history of [[museums]],<ref>{{cite book|editor-last1=Anderson|editor-first1=R. G. W.|title=Enlightening the British : knowledge, discovery and the museum in the eighteenth century|date=2003|publisher=British Museum Press|location=London|isbn=978-0714150109}}</ref> and the work of [[Joseph Black]]<ref>{{cite book|editor-last1=Anderson|editor-first1=Robert G. W.|editor-last2=Jones|editor-first2=Jean|title=The correspondence of Joseph Black|date=2012|publisher=Ashgate Pub.|location=Farnham, Surrey, England|isbn=9780754601319}}</ref> and [[Joseph Priestley]].<ref>{{cite book|editor-last1=Anderson|editor-first1=R.G.W.|editor-last2=Lawrence|editor-first2=Christopher|title=Science, medicine and dissent|date=1986|publisher=Wellcome Trust|location=London|isbn=978-0901805287}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
Anderson is a member of the [[International Academy of the History of Science]], and a Commandeur de l’Ordre des Arts et des Lettres (France).<ref name="Illinois"/> He is a [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh]] (1990),<ref name="RSE">{{cite web|title=RSE Fellows as at 05/05/2016|url=https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/lists/fellows.pdf|website=Royal Society of Edinburgh|accessdate=5 May 2016|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20160330014912/https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/lists/fellows.pdf|archivedate=30 March 2016|df=dmy-all}}</ref> the [[Society of Antiquaries of London]] (1986)<ref name="SAL">{{cite web|title=See who else is on board|url=https://www.sal.org.uk/about-us/fellows-directory/A/page/4/#directory|website=Society of Antiquaries of London|accessdate=23 May 2016}}</ref> and of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]].<ref name="Illinois"/> In 1990 he was elected Honorary Fellow<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.socantscot.org/about-us/honorary-fellows|website=www.socantscot.org|access-date=2023-09-25|title=Honorary Fellows}}</ref> of the [[Society of Antiquaries of Scotland]].

Anderson is a recipient of the [[Dexter Award]] (1986)<ref name="Ihde">{{cite journal|last1=Ihde|first1=Aaron J.|title=THE HISTORY OF THE DEXTER AWARD|journal=Bull. Hist. Chem.|date=1989|volume=4|pages=23–26|url=http://www.scs.illinois.edu/~mainzv/HIST/bulletin_open_access/num4/num4%20p23-26.pdf|accessdate=23 May 2016}}</ref> and of the [[Paul Bunge Prize]], which he was awarded in 2016 for a lifetime of "outstanding achievement in writing about and promoting the understanding of historic scientific instruments".<ref name="BungeCHF">{{cite web|title=Robert G. W. Anderson to Receive the Paul Bunge Prize|url=http://www.chemheritage.org/about/news-and-press/press-releases/2016-04-12-robert-g-w-anderson-to-receive-the-paul-bunge-prize.aspx|website=Chemical Heritage Foundation|accessdate=23 May 2016 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20160712172318/http://www.chemheritage.org/about/news-and-press/press-releases/2016-04-12-robert-g-w-anderson-to-receive-the-paul-bunge-prize.aspx|archive-date=12 July 2016}}</ref><ref>[https://idw-online.de/de/news649253 Paul-Bunge-Preis geht an Robert Anderson – Über 43 Jahre Einsatz für die Instrumentengeschichte.] Pressemitteilung vom 12. April 2016 beim [[Informationsdienst Wissenschaft]] (idw-online.de)</ref>
